content:
Today we enter Numbers chapter twelve. Israel had already begun the wilderness journey from Sinai. The people had murmured at Taberah. Then the mixed multitude had influenced Israel to crave the food of Egypt, and many died at Kibroth-hattaavah because of their greed. Now the chapter turns away from the people in general and shows us a problem that arose inside Moses' own family.

Numbers 12:1 says, "While they were at Hazeroth, Miriam and Aaron criticized Moses because he had married a Cushite woman." This was a very serious moment. Miriam and Aaron were not ordinary people in Israel. Miriam was the sister of Moses. She had watched over him when he was a baby floating in the Nile. She was also called a prophetess in Exodus 15:20, and she had led the women of Israel in praise after the great deliverance at the Red Sea. Aaron was the brother of Moses and the high priest of Israel. Both of them had been greatly used by Yahweh. Yet here, these two spoke against Moses.

The reason mentioned first is that Moses had married a Cushite woman.
Cush normally refers to the region south of Egypt, often connected with Ethiopia or Nubia, so some understand the Cushite woman to have been an African woman. Cush was also a name in the family line of Ham, for Genesis 10:6 says, "The descendants of Ham were Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan."So in the Bible, Cush is both a person and also a name connected with a people and a region south of Egypt. Some say Cushite woman is not Zipporah, Moses' Midianite wife. But Zipporah is the only wife of Moses whose marriage is actually told to us in Scripture. Exodus 2:21 says, "In time, Reuel gave Moses his daughter Zipporah to be his wife." Other scholars connect Cush with Midian, for Habakkuk 3:7 places Cushan and Midian together, saying, "I saw the people of Cushan in distress, and the nation of Midian trembling in terror." Because of this, some of the ancient Jewish interpreters also identified the Cushite woman with Zipporah. So there are two main understandings; either Moses had married another woman from Cush, or this refers to Zipporah described in a different way. The Bible does not give us all the details.

What it clearly tells us is that Miriam and Aaron used Moses' marriage as the reason for their criticism.

But the marriage was not the real heart of the matter. Numbers 12:2 reveals the deeper problem. "They said, 'Has Yahweh spoken only through Moses? Hasn't he spoken through us, too?' But Yahweh heard them." This verse shows the true issue. Miriam and Aaron were not merely concerned about Moses' wife.

They were challenging Moses' unique place and authority. They said, in effect, has Yahweh spoken only through Moses? Has He not spoken through us also? This was a question of jealousy, of pride, and of position. It is true that Yahweh had used Miriam. It is true that Yahweh had used Aaron. But Yahweh had appointed Moses in a special way. Moses was not lifting himself up.Yahweh had chosen him, called him, and used him to lead Israel out of Egypt, to receive the Law, and to speak with Yahweh in a very unique manner.And notice the last line: "But Yahweh heard them." Miriam and Aaron may have spoken only to one another, but Yahweh heard every word. Their criticism was not hidden from Him.

Then the Bible gives us a beautiful statement about Moses himself. Numbers 12:3 says, "Now Moses was very humble, more humble than any other person on earth." Moses did not rise up to defend himself. He did not argue back with Miriam and Aaron. He did not use his authority to punish them. Moses was humble, and he left the whole matter quietly in Yahweh's hands. He did not need to fight for his own place, because the One who had appointed him would defend him.

And Yahweh did act. Numbers 12:4 says, "So immediately Yahweh called to Moses, Aaron, and Miriam and said, 'Go out to the Tabernacle, all three of you!' So the three of them went to the Tabernacle." Yahweh called all three of them out. The matter had become serious, and Yahweh would now answer it directly. Numbers 12:5 says, "Then Yahweh descended in the pillar of cloud and stood at the entrance of the Tabernacle. 'Aaron and Miriam!' he called, and they stepped forward." Yahweh descended in the pillar of cloud, and Aaron and Miriam were called forward to stand before Him. Now Yahweh would explain the difference between Moses and all other prophets. He said in Numbers 12:6, "Now listen to what I say: If there were prophets among you, I, Yahweh, would reveal myself in visions. I would speak to them in dreams." Yahweh said He could speak to prophets through visions and dreams. This was real communication from Him. Prophets could receive true messages from Yahweh in this way.

But Moses was different, and here Yahweh was about to say something about His servant that Miriam and Aaron desperately needed to hear; something that would show them exactly how serious their words had been, and would leave them with no excuse for what they had done. The pillar of cloud stood at the door of the Tabernacle. Aaron and Miriam stood trembling before it. And Yahweh began to speak about the very man they had criticized. What He said next, and what happened the moment the cloud lifted, we will study tomorrow.

title: Prayer
text:
O Yahweh, our God,

We are reminded today that You hear even the words we speak in private.

Guard our hearts from jealousy and pride that hide behind other complaints.

Teach us the humility of Moses, who did not fight for his own place, but left it with You.

Help us never to speak carelessly against those You have appointed.

And when we are wronged, help us to be quiet and trust You to defend us.

"I said to myself, 'I will watch what I do and not sin in what I say.'" -

Psalm 39:1 In the name of Christ, we pray. Amen.
